balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

ebitda.title: EBITDA
ebitda.content:
EBITDA is earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation -- an operating-cash proxy that ignores capital intensity.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: read it beside CapEx: a business that must reinvest most of its EBITDA is not as cash-generative as the margin suggests.

What to watch:

  • EBITDA margin trend
  • Gap between EBITDA and operating cash flow (working capital)

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

geoVolume.title: Gold-equivalent ounces (GEO)
geoVolume.content:
GEO produced is attributable production from WPM's streaming and royalty interests, converted to a gold-equivalent basis so silver, palladium and cobalt streams sit on one comparable axis; GEO sold is what was actually delivered and invoiced in the period, which can lag production when the counterparty mine ships late in a quarter.

For Wheaton Precious Metals: WPM owns no mines -- this is pure volume risk from its streaming partners' operations, not an operating decision WPM controls directly. A gap between produced and sold is usually timing, not lost volume.

What to watch:

  • Sold consistently trailing produced for several quarters (delivery backlog)
  • New stream start-ups (e.g. Salobo, Marmato) stepping volume up
  • Mine-level disruption at a single large counterparty flowing straight through

geoMargin.title: Realized price, cash cost and margin per GEO
geoMargin.content:
Realized price per GEO is what WPM actually received per gold-equivalent ounce sold, which tracks the spot metal price. Cash cost per GEO is the price WPM pays the mine operator under its long-term purchase agreements -- typically a low, near-fixed figure (a few hundred dollars an ounce) set when the stream was originated, not a mining cost base that inflates with the operator's opex. Cash operating margin per GEO is simply realized price less cash cost.

For Wheaton Precious Metals: this spread is the entire economic engine of a streaming company -- there is no COGS, inventory or mine-operating-cost line behind it the way a miner's gross margin has. Because cash cost per ounce is contractually fixed while realized price moves with the gold and silver price, the margin expands almost linearly with metal prices: FY2024's $1,988/oz margin became FY2025's $3,040/oz on cash cost that barely moved ($438 to $514/oz) while realized price jumped from roughly $2,426 to $3,554/oz.

What to watch:

  • Cash cost per GEO creeping up (most agreements have small annual escalators)
  • Margin compression if metal prices fall -- cash cost is sticky but realized price is not
  • New streams added at a higher fixed cash cost than the existing book

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Wheaton Precious Metals Corp.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
